question: According to the manual, why should you always be looking for hazards and thinking about the emergencies they could turn into?
choice_a: So you have time to plan a way out of any emergency that develops
choice_b: It is only necessary when driving at night
choice_c: So you can safely increase your speed
choice_d: So you can stop checking your mirrors as often
explanation: You look for hazards in order to have time to plan a way out of any emergency, based on the emergencies you think the hazard could develop into.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.4 Always Have a Plan

question: What does the manual say you become by always being prepared to take action based on your hazard plans?
choice_a: A faster driver overall
choice_b: Exempt from following distance rules
choice_c: Less likely to need mirrors
choice_d: A prepared, defensive driver who improves your own safety and the safety of all road users
explanation: Being prepared to act on your plans makes you a prepared, defensive driver who will improve your own safety as well as the safety of all road users.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.8.4 Always Have a Plan

question: How does the manual define a driver distraction?
choice_a: Only a mechanical failure in the vehicle
choice_b: Anything that takes your attention away from driving
choice_c: Only conversations with passengers
choice_d: Only the use of a cell phone
explanation: The manual defines a driver distraction as anything that takes your attention away from driving.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9 Distracted Driving

question: What can distracted driving cause, according to the manual?
choice_a: Collisions resulting in injury, death, or property damage
choice_b: No measurable effect on safety
choice_c: Faster reaction times
choice_d: Improved fuel economy
explanation: Whenever your full attention is not on the driving task you put yourself, passengers, other vehicles, and pedestrians in danger, and distracted driving can cause collisions resulting in injury, death or property damage.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9 Distracted Driving

question: Which of the following is listed by the manual as an activity inside the vehicle that can distract your attention?
choice_a: Maintaining a steady following distance
choice_b: Reading maps or other literature
choice_c: Checking your mirrors as trained
choice_d: Signaling before a lane change
explanation: The manual lists reading maps or other literature, along with talking to passengers, adjusting the radio, eating or drinking, and talking or texting on a phone, as in-vehicle activities that can distract a driver's attention.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9 Distracted Driving

question: Which of the following is listed by the manual as a possible distraction that could occur outside a moving vehicle?
choice_a: A properly functioning speedometer
choice_b: An outside event such as police pulling someone over or a crash scene
choice_c: A green traffic signal
choice_d: A clear, empty roadway
explanation: The manual lists outside traffic, vehicles or pedestrians; outside events such as police pulling someone over or a crash scene; sunlight/sunset; objects in the roadway; road construction; and reading billboards as possible outside distractions.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9 Distracted Driving

question: According to the Large Truck Crash Causation Study (LTCCS) cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was externally distracted?
choice_a: 8 percent
choice_b: 39 percent
choice_c: 2 percent
choice_d: 23 percent
explanation: The LTCCS reported that 8 percent of large-truck crashes occurred when CMV drivers were externally distracted.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to the LTCCS cited in the manual, what percentage of large-truck crashes occurred when the CMV driver was internally distracted?
choice_a: 8 percent
choice_b: 12 percent
choice_c: 2 percent
choice_d: 39 percent
explanation: The LTCCS reported that 2 percent of large truck crashes occurred when the driver was internally distracted, compared to 8 percent for external distraction.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts cited in the manual, approximately how many people are killed each year on U.S. roadways in crashes involving distracted driving?
explanation: The manual states that approximately 5,500 people are killed each year on U.S. roadways in motor vehicle crashes involving distracted driving, with an estimated 448,000 injured.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts cited in the manual, approximately how many people are injured each year in crashes involving distracted driving?
explanation: The manual states an estimated 448,000 people are injured each year in motor vehicle crashes involving distracted driving, alongside approximately 5,500 killed.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: According to research cited in the manual, talking on a cell phone, even hands-free, saps the brain of what percentage of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving?
explanation: Research indicates that the burden of talking on a cell phone, even if it's hands-free, saps the brain of 39% of the energy it would ordinarily devote to safe driving.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.1 The Distracted Driving Crash Problem

question: What is one effect of distracted driving described in the manual?
choice_a: Improved reaction time
choice_b: Increased fuel efficiency
choice_c: Slowed perception, which may cause you to be delayed in perceiving or completely fail to perceive an important traffic event
choice_d: Better vehicle handling
explanation: Effects of distracted driving include slowed perception, which may delay or prevent perceiving an important traffic event.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.2 Effects of Distracted Driving

question: Besides slowed perception, what other effect of distracted driving does the manual describe?
choice_a: Permanent loss of vehicle control
choice_b: Delayed decision making and improper action, which can cause incorrect inputs to the steering, accelerator, or brakes
choice_c: Increased following distance awareness
choice_d: Automatic activation of hazard lights
explanation: Distracted driving can also cause delayed decision making and improper action, delaying proper action or causing incorrect inputs to the steering, accelerator or brakes.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.2 Effects of Distracted Driving

question: What is a 'physical distraction' as defined in the manual?
choice_a: One that only occurs at night
choice_b: One that only involves emotional stress
choice_c: One that causes you to take your hands off the wheel or eyes off the road, such as reaching for an object
choice_d: One caused solely by weather conditions
explanation: A physical distraction is one that causes you to take your hands off the wheel or eyes off the road, such as reaching for an object.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.3 Types of Distractions

question: What is a 'mental distraction' as defined in the manual?
choice_a: Only distractions caused by loud noises
choice_b: Only distractions from other vehicles
choice_c: A distraction that always involves texting
choice_d: Activities that take your mind away from the road, such as engaging in conversation with a passenger
explanation: A mental distraction is defined as activities that take your mind away from the road, such as conversation with a passenger or thinking about something that happened during the day.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.3 Types of Distractions

question: Why does the manual treat talking on a cell phone or sending/reading text messages as an even greater crash risk than a purely physical or purely mental distraction?
choice_a: Because it is illegal in all vehicles, commercial or not
choice_b: Because it involves both physical and mental distraction at the same time
choice_c: Because it has no effect on reaction time
choice_d: Because it only affects new drivers
explanation: Both physical and mental distraction together create an even greater chance a crash could happen, such as talking on a cell phone or sending/reading text messages.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.3 Types of Distractions

question: What do the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) cited in the manual do regarding hand-held mobile telephones?
choice_a: Only apply to passenger vehicles, not CMVs
choice_b: Ban all mobile phones, hands-free or not, in every situation
choice_c: Restrict the use of hand-held mobile telephones by CMV drivers and prohibit motor carriers from requiring or allowing such use
choice_d: Only apply to drivers under age 21
explanation: 49 CFR Parts 383, 384, 390, 391 and 392 restrict the use of hand-held mobile telephones by CMV drivers, and motor carriers are prohibited from requiring or allowing drivers of CMVs to use hand-held mobile telephones.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: According to the manual, which of the following counts as 'use of a hand-held mobile telephone'?
choice_a: Listening to the radio
choice_b: Dialing a mobile telephone by pressing more than a single button
choice_c: Glancing at a mounted GPS screen
choice_d: Checking a mirror
explanation: The use of a hand-held mobile telephone includes holding it with at least one hand to conduct a voice communication, dialing by pressing more than a single button, or moving from a seated, restrained position to reach for the phone.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: If you choose to use a mobile phone while operating a CMV, what type of phone use is permitted under the rule described in the manual?
choice_a: Any hand-held device, as long as it is used briefly
choice_b: Texting only, never voice calls
choice_c: Any phone use is completely prohibited with no exceptions
choice_d: Only a hands-free mobile phone located close to you that can be operated to conduct a voice communication
explanation: If a driver chooses to use a mobile phone while operating a CMV, they may only use a hands-free mobile phone located close to them that can be operated in compliance with the rule to conduct a voice communication.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How many convictions of hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV will result in CDL disqualification, according to the manual?
choice_a: Five convictions
choice_b: One conviction
choice_c: Two or more convictions
choice_d: Convictions never result in disqualification for this offense
explanation: A CDL will be disqualified after two or more convictions of any state law on hand-held mobile telephone use while operating a CMV.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: What is the CDL disqualification period for a second hand-held mobile phone offense within 3 years, according to the manual?
choice_a: 30 days
choice_b: 1 year
choice_c: 120 days
choice_d: 60 days
explanation: Disqualification is 60 days for the second hand-held mobile telephone offense within 3 years, and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Up to how much can a driver be civilly penalized for a hand-held mobile telephone violation while operating a CMV, according to the manual?
explanation: Each violation of the hand-held mobile telephone prohibition subjects the driver to civil penalties in an amount up to $2,750.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Up to how much can a motor carrier/employer be civilly penalized for allowing or requiring a driver to use a hand-held mobile telephone while driving, according to the manual?
explanation: Employers may be subject to civil penalties in an amount up to $11,000 for allowing or requiring drivers to use hand-held mobile telephones while driving.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Does the hand-held mobile telephone restriction have any exception, according to the manual?
choice_a: Yes, an emergency exception allows use to communicate with law enforcement or other emergency services
choice_b: No exceptions exist under any circumstance
choice_c: Yes, but only when the vehicle is empty of cargo
choice_d: Yes, but only for calls under 30 seconds
explanation: There is an emergency exception that allows drivers to use hand-held mobile telephones if necessary to communicate with law enforcement officials or other emergency services.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: According to research cited in the manual, how many times greater are the odds of a safety-critical event for CMV drivers who dial a mobile telephone while driving compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 2 times greater
choice_b: 23.2 times greater
choice_c: 6 times greater
choice_d: 10 times greater
explanation: The odds of being involved in a safety-critical event, such as a crash or near-crash, are 6 times greater for CMV drivers who dial a mobile telephone while driving than for those who do not.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: According to the manual, how far does a driver traveling 55 mph go while taking their eyes off the road for the average 3.8 seconds it takes to dial a mobile telephone?
choice_a: About 500 feet
choice_b: About 50 feet
choice_c: About 150 feet
choice_d: About 306 feet, roughly the length of a football field
explanation: Dialing drivers took their eyes off the forward roadway for an average of 3.8 seconds; at 55 mph (80.7 feet per second) this equates to traveling 306 feet, about the length of a football field.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: Are hands-free cell phone devices less likely to cause distraction than hand-held devices, according to the manual?
choice_a: Yes, hands-free devices eliminate all distraction
choice_b: No, hands-free devices are no less likely than hand-held phones to cause distraction because attention is diverted from the driving task either way
choice_c: Hands-free devices are only safe at low speeds
choice_d: Hands-free devices are safer only in daylight
explanation: The manual notes that hands-free devices are no less likely than hand-held cell phones to cause you to become distracted, since attention is diverted from the driving task while using either device.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.4 Cell/Mobile Phones

question: How does the manual define 'texting' for purposes of the federal CMV driving prohibition?
choice_a: Manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including SMS, e-mail, instant messaging, or accessing a web page
choice_b: Any use of a GPS navigation system
choice_c: Only sending a text message via SMS
choice_d: Only using a laptop computer while driving
explanation: Texting means manually entering text into, or reading text from, an electronic device, including short message service, e-mailing, instant messaging, or a command to access a World Wide Web page.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: What is the CDL disqualification period for a driver's second texting-while-driving offense within 3 years, according to the manual?
choice_a: 90 days
choice_b: 30 days
choice_c: 60 days
choice_d: 180 days
explanation: Disqualification is 60 days for a second texting offense within 3 years, and 120 days for three or more offenses within 3 years, the same structure as the hand-held phone violation.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: Up to how much can a driver be civilly penalized for a texting-while-driving violation while operating a CMV, according to the manual?
explanation: The first and each subsequent violation of the texting prohibition is subject to civil penalties on the driver in an amount up to $2,750.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: Is there an emergency exception to the texting prohibition for CMV drivers, according to the manual?
choice_a: Yes, but only to family members
choice_b: Yes, but only while the vehicle is parked with the engine off
choice_c: No exception exists
choice_d: Yes, an emergency exception allows texting if necessary to communicate with law enforcement or other emergency services
explanation: There is an emergency exception that allows a driver to text if necessary to communicate with law enforcement officials or other emergency services.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: Why does the manual state that texting is even riskier than talking on a cell phone?
choice_a: Texting is not actually riskier than talking
choice_b: Texting is only possible while stopped
choice_c: Texting requires looking at a small screen and manipulating the keypad, involving both physical and mental distraction simultaneously
choice_d: Texting uses more battery power than calling
explanation: Evidence suggests text messaging is even riskier than talking on a cell phone because it requires looking at a small screen and manipulating the keypad, making it the most alarming distraction since it involves both physical and mental distraction simultaneously.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: According to research cited in the manual, how many times greater are the odds of a safety-critical event for CMV drivers who text while driving compared to those who do not?
choice_a: 15 times greater
choice_b: 23.2 times greater
choice_c: 6 times greater
choice_d: 10 times greater
explanation: The odds of being involved in a safety-critical event are 23.2 times greater for CMV drivers who engage in texting while driving than for those who do not.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: On average, how many seconds does sending or receiving a text take a driver's eyes from the road, and how far does that carry them at 55 mph, according to the manual?
choice_a: 4.6 seconds, about 371 feet, the length of a football field
choice_b: 2.1 seconds, about 150 feet
choice_c: 6.0 seconds, about 500 feet
choice_d: 3.8 seconds, about 306 feet
explanation: Sending or receiving text takes a driver's eyes from the road for an average of 4.6 seconds, or 371 feet at 55 mph, the length of an entire football field.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.5 Texting

question: What is your goal regarding in-vehicle distractions before driving begins, according to the manual?
choice_a: To minimize distractions only on highways
choice_b: To eliminate all in-vehicle distractions before driving begins
choice_c: Distractions cannot be reduced, so no goal is stated
choice_d: To identify distractions only after they occur
explanation: The manual states your goal should be to eliminate all in-vehicle distractions before driving begins, accomplished by assessing potential distractions and developing a preventative plan.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: What happens to crash risk if drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, according to the manual?
choice_a: Crashes double
choice_b: Crashes triple only in bad weather
choice_c: There is no measurable effect
choice_d: Crashes decrease slightly
explanation: The manual states that if drivers react a half-second slower because of distractions, crashes double.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: Which of the following is listed by the manual as a tip to avoid becoming a distracted driver?
choice_a: Keep the radio and CDs unset until you are already driving
choice_b: Wait to review your route until you are on the road
choice_c: Turn off all communication devices
choice_d: Leave loose cargo unsecured
explanation: Among the tips the manual lists to avoid becoming distracted is to turn off all communication devices.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: If you must use a mobile phone while driving, what does the manual recommend?
choice_a: Only use it while changing lanes
choice_b: Set it on the floor of the cab
choice_c: Hold it in one hand while steering with the other
choice_d: Make sure it is within close proximity, operable while restrained, and use an earpiece, speaker phone, voice-activated dialing, or the hands-free feature
explanation: The manual recommends that if you must use a mobile phone, make sure it is within close proximity, that it is operable while restrained, and use an earpiece, speaker phone function, voice-activated dialing, or the hands-free feature.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: Are drivers considered in compliance if they unsafely reach for a mobile phone but intend to use its hands-free function, according to the manual?
choice_a: Yes, as long as the phone is answered within one ring
choice_b: Yes, intent to use hands-free always makes it compliant
choice_c: Compliance only depends on vehicle speed
choice_d: No, drivers are not in compliance if they unsafely reach for a mobile phone, even if they intend to use the hands-free feature
explanation: The manual states drivers are not in compliance if they unsafely reach for a mobile phone, even if they intend to use the hands-free function.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

question: What does the manual recommend regarding conversations with other occupants of the vehicle?
choice_a: Conversations with passengers have no effect on driving safety
choice_b: Encourage passengers to debate controversial topics to stay alert
choice_c: Only the driver should speak during the trip
choice_d: Don't engage in complex or emotionally intense conversations with other occupants
explanation: The manual advises not engaging in complex or emotionally intense conversations with other occupants, and securing their commitment to behave responsibly and support the driver in reducing distractions.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.6 Don't Drive Distracted

topic: Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers
question: Why is it important to be able to recognize other drivers who are engaged in driving distraction, according to the manual?
choice_a: Not recognizing other distracted drivers can prevent you from perceiving or reacting correctly in time to prevent a crash
choice_b: It has no bearing on your own safety
choice_c: It allows you to legally pass them at any speed
choice_d: It is required only for new drivers
explanation: The manual explains that not recognizing other distracted drivers can prevent you from perceiving or reacting correctly in time to prevent a crash.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.7 Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers

topic: Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers
question: Which of the following is listed by the manual as a clue that another driver may be distracted?
choice_a: A vehicle maintaining a constant, steady speed
choice_b: Vehicles that drift over the lane divider lines or within their own lane
choice_c: A vehicle coming to a complete stop at a stop sign
choice_d: A vehicle using its turn signal well in advance
explanation: The manual lists vehicles drifting over the lane divider lines or within their own lane, vehicles traveling at inconsistent speeds, and drivers preoccupied with maps, food, cigarettes, or cell phones as clues of a distracted driver.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.7 Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers

topic: Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers
question: What does the manual advise you do when you notice a distracted driver near you?
choice_a: Flash your high beams repeatedly until they notice you
choice_b: Give the distracted driver plenty of room and maintain your safe following distance
choice_c: Pull directly alongside them to get their attention
choice_d: Follow as closely as possible to avoid separation
explanation: The manual advises giving a distracted driver plenty of room and maintaining your safe following distance.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.7 Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers

topic: Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers
question: Why does the manual say to be very careful when passing a driver who seems to be distracted?
choice_a: The other driver may not be aware of your presence and may drift in front of you
choice_b: Passing a distracted driver is always illegal
choice_c: It has no special risk compared to passing any other driver
choice_d: Distracted drivers always speed up when passed
explanation: The manual warns to be very careful passing a driver who seems distracted because they may not be aware of your presence and may drift in front of you.
source_note: Minnesota Commercial Driver's License Manual (Modernized Testing System, AAMVA base content Version: July 2017), Minnesota Department of Public Safety (DPS), Division of Driver and Vehicle Services (DVS) -- Section 2, Driving Safely, 2.9.7 Watch Out for Other Distracted Drivers
